If we look closely at the direction taken by Muʿtazilite discussions of the divine “attributes”—the group of questions centered on the principle of divine unity—the picture becomes clearer.

All this intense intellectual effort was directed toward establishing divine unity on an extremely firm foundation: the absolute transcendence of God, placing the divine being completely beyond comparison with the created world and completely above it.
This absolute transcendence stood at the center of the ideology of Islam—that is, of the social and political order of the Islamic state.

The social, or more precisely social-political, meaning of this transcendent concept of divine unity, as the Muʿtazilites developed it, pointed toward an image of an enormous distance between the person at the head of the Islamic state—the caliph—and the institutions of the state on one side, and the human members of Arab-Islamic society on the other.
That distance mirrored the vast separation between the transcendent and unique divine being and our material world.
This was the basic foundation of the ideological structure of the caliphal state.

Does this mean, then, that when the Muʿtazilites struggled intellectually to establish divine unity on the basis of absolute transcendence, they were also helping to create an ideology of absolute separation between the head of the caliphal system and the society ruled by that system—between an absolute ruler and those he ruled?
Broadly speaking, there is no doubt that they moved within the limits of this ideology, whether they intended to or not, and whether they were conscious of it or not.

The social and intellectual conditions of their time, and the objective historical relationships within those conditions, placed them in a position to produce the ideology of the caliphal system in a rational form.

But because thought has its own internal movement and a degree of relative independence, producing the ideology of the system in this rational form also meant producing contradictions within that ideology at the same time.
We have already seen several examples of this contradiction in the present chapter on divine unity.
The most important was the breakthrough made in what we might call the Islamic theory of knowledge.
The Muʿtazilites opened more and more space for reason to enter fields of inquiry, investigation, and discovery that had previously been closed to it.
As reason pushed into these new areas, further contradictions within the ideology of the established order began to appear.
We saw this in al-Naẓẓām’s system of thought.
And we will see it again in the chapter on justice, to which we now turn.

“...The title most closely associated with the Muʿtazilites, even in their later period when their thinking turned to questions in which philosophy and kalām overlapped, was ‘the People of Justice.’ They held that no evil comes from God, and that He rewards or punishes people according to what they themselves have done.”

It was no accident that the followers of the Muʿtazilite school as a whole came to be known as the “People of Justice.” After all, belief in divine justice lies at the heart of Islam for all Muslim groups and schools. In the previous chapter, we saw that it was equally significant that the Muʿtazilites were called the “People of Divine Unity,” even though belief in God’s oneness is also a basic principle shared by all Muslims.
The reason is that the Muʿtazilites did not understand divine justice in the simple sense accepted by the earliest Muslims, or in the later traditionalist sense, which was defined like this:

“God is just in His actions because He has full authority over what belongs to Him. He does whatever He wishes and judges however He wishes. Justice means putting a thing in its proper place, and this means dealing with what belongs to Him according to His will and knowledge. Injustice is the opposite. It is therefore impossible for Him”—that is, for God—“to judge unjustly or act wrongly in what is His.”

What this definition seems to mean is that justice rests on faith in the idea that God’s absolute will never puts anything in the wrong place. The traditionalist idea of justice therefore comes down to “putting a thing in its proper place.”

But this remains extremely general and open-ended. The standard used to decide what the “proper place” of something is remains absolute as well, because in the end everything goes back to God’s will: “He does whatever He wishes and judges however He wishes.”
We are therefore dealing with a vague idea of justice grounded entirely in faith in the religious texts themselves, without reason playing any independent part in defining it.

The Muʿtazilites tried to do something different. They subjected the idea of divine justice to rational interpretation and gave it a theoretical treatment drawing on both kalām and philosophy. In doing so, they tried to define the relationship between God’s actions and human actions—and, as we will see, even the actions of nature.

De Boer summed up this theoretical development in the statement quoted at the beginning of this discussion. In the Muʿtazilite view, divine justice could only make sense within Islamic belief if the relationship between God and human beings was understood in a way that allowed people to choose their own actions. Only then could a person be responsible for what they did, and only then could God’s reward or punishment follow from that responsibility.

If human beings had no choice in what they did, the Muʿtazilites argued, they could not be held responsible for their actions, whether good or bad. If they were not responsible, then reward would be pointless and arbitrary, while punishment would be unjust.
Both absurdity and injustice are forms of evil. And no evil comes from God.

For the Muʿtazilites, then, divine justice had a very specific meaning. It rested on a logically ordered argument built on two principles: first, evil does not come from God; second, rewarding or punishing someone for an act they did not freely choose would itself be evil.
But beneath these two principles lay the larger and more basic issue that had given rise to this whole way of thinking: human freedom of will and action.

The Qadarites, who were the intellectual predecessors of the Muʿtazilites, had rejected predestination and defended human freedom from a directly political starting point. Its content was almost class-based, even though its outward form was religious, as we explained earlier.

By the time the Muʿtazilites entered the period of systematic kalām and philosophical thought, however, the question had become somewhat independent of that original political setting. It had developed into a theoretical intellectual problem in its own right. The Muʿtazilites built a logical system around it, and then developed further theories based on concepts organized in much the same way.
2 — The Social Basis of the Idea of Justice
None of this means that the original social and political roots of the issue disappeared from Muʿtazilite thought.
Throughout the period when their kalām was developing, the social basis of their thinking remained present, even if it is not always easy to see at first glance.

It is striking that most of the leading Muʿtazilite thinkers—and especially those who were most committed to reason, human freedom, and the rejection of predestination—came from the social group known as the mawālī.

The mawālī occupied a lower social position in Arab society than people who were not mawālī. Some had been slaves. Some had been enslaved after capture in war. Others had become dependants of particular tribes through alliances in which the weaker party became so closely attached to the stronger that the relationship could extend even to genealogy.
Almost every major Muʿtazilite thinker carried some version of the description “mawlā of so-and-so” or “mawlā of such-and-such tribe or clan,” even at the height of his intellectual reputation.

It is difficult to imagine that this did not make such men aware, at some level, of the limits placed on their social standing. And it is quite possible that this experience influenced parts of their intellectual outlook even if they were not consciously aware of it.
Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, for example, was followed by this label throughout the historical tradition and is still described by modern researchers as “a mawlā of ʿAbd al-Qays.”
The same is true of al-Naẓẓām. Despite his enormous intellectual stature, even modern writers continue to mention that “he was one of the mawālī.”
The same applies to al-Jāḥiẓ, who was said to have been a mawlā of the Kināna tribe.
So al-Baghdādī’s statement that creative excellence in every field came from the children of slaves was not without some basis in the actual history of Arab intellectual life.
At this point, the logic of our investigation allows us to ask a question:
Could this historical and social reality have played some part in the development of the Muʿtazilite idea of justice?
There is good reason to ask.

Human freedom is one of the two main foundations of the Muʿtazilite idea of justice. We are not claiming that the social influence we are describing was something the Muʿtazilites consciously recognized. Nor are we claiming that it acted directly.

What we are suggesting is that their social position may have worked quietly beneath the surface and helped shape their strong attachment to human freedom and their rejection of a mysterious destiny imposed from above.

We have already seen that this rejection had an ideological side. Historical evidence shows that belief in divine decree and predestination often expressed the ideology of a particular ruling class. The Umayyad rulers defended the idea strongly and used it against their opponents, especially the early Qadarites such as Maʿbad al-Juhanī and Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.

We may be able to see another trace of this social reality in some of the Muʿtazilites’ known political positions, whether toward events in their own time or toward earlier conflicts from the first period of Islam.
For example, they agreed that Muʿāwiya was wrong to fight ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.
Some of them also criticized the third Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUthmān, saying:

“He placed the Umayyads over the necks of the people, appointed them to governorships, and granted them landed estates. Armenia was conquered during his reign, and he took the entire fifth of the spoils and gave it to Marwān. He reserved the grazing lands around Medina from the livestock of the Muslims, except for those of the Umayyads. And on the same day that he ordered one hundred thousand from the public treasury to be given to Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam, he gave Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb”—Muʿāwiya’s father—“two hundred thousand from the Muslims’ treasury...”
An even clearer example of the social basis of Muʿtazilite thought can be found in the political position taken by some of them on the question of leadership.

Some accepted the Khārijite view that the imam did not have to come from Quraysh. Others went even further. One Muʿtazilite argued that if a Qurashī Arab and a non-Arab were equally qualified, the non-Arab should be made imam.
This was the opinion of Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr. He explained his reasoning by saying that the non-Arab would have fewer powerful relatives around him.
The political and social meaning of this argument is clear.

It points directly to a criticism often made of many caliphs, including the criticism of ʿUthmān quoted above: rulers used the benefits of political power for their own relatives and clans, giving them preference over the rest of the population.
The following passage from al-Ashʿarī may give us a useful way into the relationship between Muʿtazilite political thought and Muʿtazilite intellectual thought. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī writes:

“They disagreed about how numerous and powerful they would need to be before they were required to rise against the ruler and fight the Muslims. The Muʿtazilites said: If we form a group and believe that we are strong enough to overcome our opponents, we appoint an imam, rise up, kill the ruler and remove him, and compel the people to accept our teaching. If they accept our view of divine unity and our view of divine decree, then so be it. If not, we fight them. The Muʿtazilites therefore made rebellion against the ruler obligatory whenever they had the opportunity and the power to do so.”
This passage gives us a clear picture of the Muʿtazilite position on political authority.
They were prepared to seek power so that they could put their ideas into practice, even by violent means, if they believed they had enough strength to succeed.

Another passage from al-Ashʿarī tells us something equally important. When the Muʿtazilites developed their particular idea of divine justice, they were also thinking about its relationship to another kind of justice: justice as something embodied in actual human relations, and therefore in real political and religious authority.

Al-Ashʿarī tells us that Muslims disagreed over whether a political uprising could take place without an imam, and whether punishments such as cutting off the hand of a thief, carrying out retaliatory punishment, and enforcing legal judgments could take place without one.
According to him, most Muʿtazilites said:

“There can be no uprising except under a just imam. And no one may enforce judgments, cut off the hand of a thief, or carry out retaliation except the just imam or someone acting on his orders. Nothing else is permitted.”
So the Muʿtazilites believed that political and religious authority had to be led by an imam, and that this imam had to be just.
But what did justice mean here?

From the earlier passage, where they speak of rising against a ruler and removing him by force, we can see that the justice they demanded from an imam included acceptance of their own views on divine unity and divine decree.

And since their view of divine decree was inseparable from their belief in human freedom—that is, from their rejection of a predetermined fate that removes human choice—we can conclude that their worldly idea of justice was also closely tied to human freedom.

This allows us to see a connection within Muʿtazilite thought between their metaphysical idea of justice, meaning divine justice, and their practical, earthly idea of justice embodied in the just imam—that is, in a political and religious authority that was socially just.

Seen in this way, Muʿtazilite “rationalism” was not simply an abstract and purely metaphysical rationalism. It also had a practical side rooted in real human life, even when that side does not appear directly in their theoretical discussions.
3 — The Main Questions Raised by Muʿtazilite Justice

The Muʿtazilites’ particular understanding of divine justice led to a number of further questions. These occupied the thinkers of their own age and later became major subjects in both old and modern studies of Muʿtazilite thought.
The most important of these questions concerned the limits of God’s power and the limits of human power over human actions.
A — The Limits of Divine Power

The Muʿtazilites had established that both good and evil human actions come from the human being, in keeping with their understanding of divine justice, which makes people responsible for everything they do.
This means that human freedom places a limit on God’s power over human action.

But does this mean that God is unable to commit evil or sinful acts? Or does it mean that He is able to do them but chooses not to because doing so would violate justice as the Muʿtazilites understood it?
Muʿtazilite thinkers did not agree on the answer.
Most of them said that God has the power to commit evil and sinful acts, but does not do so because such acts are wrong.

ʿAbbād ibn Sulaymān and his followers expressed the matter differently. They said that God has the power over injustice and wrongdoing, but they would not say that He has the power to act unjustly or to do wrong.
This wording shows the intellectual difficulty they were facing.
They were trying to reconcile two ideas: that God’s power—indeed, God’s very being—embraces everything, and that human beings freely choose their own actions.
ʿAbbād’s solution seems to avoid the problem by playing with the wording rather than truly resolving it.
He argued that God cannot be described as having the power to commit evil or sinful acts at all. Such acts are simply not within His power.
His argument was that if wrongness belongs to the evil act itself, and this is what prevents us from attributing the act to God, then:
“To allow that an evil act could come from Him would itself be evil.”
